Part of #18300
Adds a table property encryption.kms-key-generation-enabled (default false).
When enabled, the key encryption key is generated by the KMS via generateKey()
instead of being created locally and wrapped via wrapKey(). If it is enabled but
the configured KeyManagementClient does not support key generation, creating a key
encryption key fails with an exception. The default keeps the current behavior.
Changes:

TableProperties: new property and default
EncryptionUtil: read the property, and treat it as an encryption property
that is invalid before format v3
StandardEncryptionManager: choose generateKey() vs wrapKey() when creating a KEK
and fail if generation is enabled but unsupported; the 4-arg constructor is
deprecated in favor of a new one that takes the flag
Hive: read the property from the HMS table parameters (like encryption.key-id
and encryption.data-key-length) rather than from the metadata file, so it
cannot be tampered with; for a new table it is taken from the table properties.
It is also part of the metadata/HMS consistency check
docs: document the new property in configuration.md

Tests: new TestStandardEncryptionManagerKeyGeneration covering default, enabled,
enabled with an unsupported client (fails), toggling the property, the table
property path, and the v2 check; new TestHiveTableKmsKeyGeneration covering the
HMS parameter path for created and loaded tables, the default, and the HMS value
taking precedence over the metadata file.
Follow-up (agreed in the review): local keys use encryption.data-key-length,
while a KMS generated key uses the KMS client's own key spec (e.g. AWS
kms.data-key-spec, default AES_256). An encryption.kek-length property will be
added in a separate PR to make this consistent.

An equality delete's match condition depends only on its equality_ids columns.
Per spec, the file may legitimately carry additional columns of
the deleted row, but their stats describe values that play no part in
the match condition.

      iceberg/format/spec.md

         Line 1633
      in
      2856631

           Equality delete files identify deleted rows in a collection of data files by one or more column values, and may optionally contain additional columns of the deleted row.

InclusiveMetricsEvaluator and StrictMetricsEvaluator evaluated the scan's row filter
against all of a delete file's column stats, so a predicate on a non-key column could
incorrectly prune a delete manifest entry (inclusive) or cause it to be dropped from the
manifest entirely (strict), leaving a row that should have been deleted in the query result.
Narrow stats to a file's equality_ids columns before metrics evaluation for equality delete files.
Additional context
https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#equality-delete-files
Equality delete files identify deleted rows in a collection of data files by one or more column values, and may optionally contain additional columns of the deleted row.
Is there a specific writer that does this (spark? flink? something else?)
Oracle GoldenGate
Issue found through trinodb/trino trinodb/trino#31399
title: Api: Don't prune equality delete manifest entries by non-key column stats

body:
Fixes #17650.
Root cause. CompareSchemasVisitor.struct() computes the merged field result as:
fields.stream().reduce(Result::merge).orElse(Result.SCHEMA_UPDATE_NEEDED)
For a zero-field struct the reduce is empty, so the fallback fires: any schema containing an empty struct (for example an Avro zero-field marker record) can never compare SAME against any table schema, not even an identical one. In the Dynamic Sink that turns into a commit/re-compare loop and ends in TableMetadataCache caching NOT_FOUND, whose null schema then NPEs in DynamicSinkUtil.getEqualityFieldIds.
Fix. SAME is the identity element of Result.merge (merge takes the max severity), so an empty struct contributes SAME and the existing table-side checks (field counts, name order, required-field coverage) still catch real differences. One-line change in each of the three Flink versions (1.20, 2.2, 2.3), whose copies of this class are identical.
Tests. Added three regression tests to TestCompareSchemasVisitor in each version:

testEmptyStructSame: identical schemas with an empty struct field compare SAME
testNestedEmptyStructSame: same for an empty struct nested in another struct
testEmptyStructAgainstNonEmptyTableStruct: empty input struct vs a table struct with an extra optional field still yields DATA_CONVERSION_NEEDED

All 26 tests in TestCompareSchemasVisitor pass (23 existing plus the 3 new).
Disclosure: prepared with AI assistance; the change was compiled and unit-tested before opening.
title: Flink: Fix CompareSchemasVisitor never returning SAME for empty structs

DeleteFileIndex keeps the file_path bounds and stats of every v2 position delete. For a file-scoped delete both bounds hold the same path, which the index only needs to find the referenced data file. body:
Closes: #16758
Problem
When downstream query engines (such as StarRocks, Trino, or Spark) cancel or abort a REST table scan early due to client disconnects, timeouts, or query limits, they trigger the cleanup sequence on the outer execution container.
In Apache Iceberg, ScanTaskIterable.close() was implemented as an empty no-op method. Because this outer close() call failed to cascade the shutdown signal to the underlying data structures:

The internal shutdown state atomic flag remained false.
Background PlanTaskWorker threads continued running indefinitely.
Once the internal taskQueue reached its 1000 item capacity limit, all active worker threads became permanently deadlocked inside offerWithTimeout(), leading to thread pool exhaustion on the engine coordinator side.

Solution

Implemented State Tracking and Cleanup: Added thread-safe execution barriers inside ScanTaskIterable.close() utilizing shutdown.compareAndSet(false, true).
Queue Eviction Matrix: Updated the close block to explicitly flush taskQueue, planTasks, and initialFileScanTasks lists upon termination. This allows background threads stuck in an offer wait cycle to instantly unblock, evaluate the flipped shutdown state, and exit gracefully.
Decoupled Iterator Lifecycle: Refactored the internal ScanTasksIterator.close() block to eliminate redundant code duplication, rewriting it to delegate its cleanup tasks straight up to ScanTaskIterable.this.close(). This ensures unified thread termination safety across all potential entry points.
Regression Test Addition: Designed and integrated TestScanTaskIterableLeak under the org.apache.iceberg.rest test package, proving that active planning thread allocations successfully scale back down to 0 upon premature termination.

Verification Testing

BaseMetastoreTableOperations and BaseViewOperations retry reading the metadata file during a refresh for up to a hard-coded 10 minutes. When the object store is reachable but unhealthy, for example when reads time out, a single loadTable blocks for about 10 minutes before it fails. body:
Closes #18499
Problem
TableMetadataCache.schema() iterates all historical table schemas in ascending schema id order and returns the first one that CompareSchemasVisitor marks as SAME. The visitor matches by field name, so after a column is dropped and re-added (or renamed and its name reused), an older schema whose field names now belong to different field ids can win over the current schema. The writer then writes data under retired or unrelated field ids, and readers using the current schema see null (or the values land in the wrong column).
Fix

The table schemas are stored in the cache in resolution order: current schema first, then the rest from newest to oldest (orderSchemas). The current schema goes first explicitly because after a rollback it is not necessarily the one with the highest id.
The ordered schemas are split into two tiers (schemaTiers). Schemas that use a field name which belongs to a different field id in the current schema are only tried when no schema of the first tier matches the input. So the current schema wins even when it needs DATA_CONVERSION_NEEDED, instead of an older schema winning with an exact match.
Old records that fit only an older schema still fall back to it, for example a dropped column that was not re-added, or a column whose type was changed externally (the case @mxm raised).

The tiered approach is based on @pvary's proposal (pvary/iceberg@f322d30), cherry-picked to keep his authorship.
This PR targets Flink 2.3 only. I will backport to Flink 1.20 and 2.2 after this is merged.
Testing
TestTableMetadataCache:

testSchemaPrefersCurrentSchemaWhenColumnIsReAddedAfterAnotherChange: add c, drop c, add d, re-add c; the old-shape record resolves to the current field id.
testSchemaPrefersCurrentSchemaWhenColumnIsReAddedWithWiderType: c int dropped and re-added as long; resolves to the current schema.
testSchemaPrefersCurrentSchemaWhenFieldNameIsReusedAfterRename: data renamed to legacy, new data added; resolves to the new data field id.
testSchemaFallsBackToHistoricalSchemaWhenReAddedColumnTypeIsIncompatible: string column re-added as double; the old record still falls back to the old schema.
Existing tests kept, including the ordering test and the "dropped and not re-added" test.

The first three fail without the tiering change. The whole org.apache.iceberg.flink.sink.dynamic test package and spotlessCheck pass on Flink 2.3.

body:
Repro for a case where a Spark Streaming data file ends up with different contents than the manifest says (record count, bounds).
Sequence of events:

Epoch N runs. Tasks write files named {partitionId}-{taskId}-{queryId}-{epochId}-{fileCount}.parquet.
Iceberg commits the snapshot for epoch N, with the files and their stats in the manifest.
The driver dies before Spark writes the checkpoint commit log entry for N.
Driver restarts on the same checkpoint. Offset log has N, commit log doesn't, so Spark replays N.
taskAttemptId is a per-SparkContext counter that restarts from 0 on the new driver. If a replay task lands on the same counter value as the original (e.g. the first batch of a scheduled AvailableNow run), it gets the same partitionId and taskId, so the same file name.
The replay can assign different rows to that partition (shuffle, AQE coalescing), and data writers use overwrite, so the committed file at that path is replaced.
commit(N) sees epochId <= lastCommittedEpochId and skips. Nothing is cleaned up or flagged.
Table now points at a file whose rows don't match its manifest entry.

The test does 1, 2 and 4 to 6 directly against the streaming writer, then checks the committed file's row count against the manifest. It fails on current code. Fix not included.
Maybe some more randomness in the file name is required? Haven';t fully thought through this though.

JdbcTableOperations and JdbcViewOperations refresh metadata with refreshFromMetadataLocation(newLocation), which retries reading the metadata file 20 times for up to 10 minutes. When the object store is reachable but unhealthy, for example when reads time out, a single loadTable blocks for up to 10 minutes before it fails. In a REST catalog server backed by JdbcCatalog, this holds a request thread for the whole time, while clients usually give up much earlier.
This is similar to #3379, which made the number of metadata refresh retries configurable for HiveTableOperations (iceberg.hive.metadata-refresh-max-retries).

Add the metadata-refresh.max-retries property to CatalogProperties. The default is 20, so behavior doesn't change.
JdbcTableOperations and JdbcViewOperations read the property from the catalog properties, reject negative values, and pass it to the existing refreshFromMetadataLocation overloads.
Document the property for the JDBC catalog.

The property is in CatalogProperties rather than prefixed with jdbc., following the review feedback in #10002 that this setting shouldn't be specific to one catalog. Other catalogs can read it the same way. It is still only wired up for JDBC to keep this PR small. Earlier attempts were #5688 and #10002.
Each retry is a full metadata read, so the total time also depends on the FileIO's own timeouts and retries (for example s3.retry.num-retries and http-client.apache.socket-timeout-ms for S3FileIO). With those bounded, this property bounds the total time of a refresh.

Closes #18556
SparkBatch.equals compares the hash code of the scan that created the batch, so Spark treats the batches of scans whose hash codes collide as equal and reuses one scan's exchange for the other, returning wrong rows. The issue has a reproduction with 'Aa' and 'BB' filters in a UNION ALL.
Each scan now lists the values that define its equality once, in equalityKey(). SparkScan implements equals and hashCode over that list (SparkChangelogScan, which does not extend it, does the same), and toBatch() passes the list to SparkBatch in place of the hash code. The batch compares the values as they were when it was created, as it did with the hash code, so a runtime filter applied to the scan afterwards does not change the batch's equality. The scans' own equality and hash codes are unchanged.
TestSparkScan covers batch equality for scans whose hash codes collide and the UNION ALL result from the issue; both fail without the change.

body:
Fixes #18552.
Problem
In POST /v1/{prefix}/transactions/commit, multi-table transactions can specify requirements on tables that are not updated (e.g. read-only cross-table assertions or key dependency checks).
Previously, requirements were only evaluated in-memory during initial staging; because tables without updates never execute an underlying commit (base == current in BaseTransaction), their requirements were not re-checked against refreshed table metadata at commit time.
Furthermore, concurrent multi-table commits against the catalog were not isolated, allowing concurrent transactions asserting contradictory states to both commit successfully.
Solution

Add CatalogHandlers.commitTransaction(Catalog, CommitTransactionRequest) with catalog-level synchronization to serialize multi-table transaction commits against the catalog.
Re-validate requirements for tables with empty updates against refreshed metadata in the catalog prior to committing.
Update RESTCatalogAdapter to delegate commitTransaction to CatalogHandlers.
Add comprehensive unit tests in TestRESTCatalog:

multipleDiffsWithRequirementOnlyTable: Verifies valid requirement-only tables commit cleanly alongside update tables.
multipleDiffsWithRequirementOnlyTableFails: Verifies stale requirements on requirement-only tables fail with CommitFailedException and prevent all table commits in the transaction.
concurrentCommitTransactionsWithCrossRequirementOnlyTables: Verifies concurrent conflicting multi-table transactions (reproducing the scenario from #18552) cannot both commit.

body:
TableUpdater.findOrCreateBranch (Flink dynamic sink) no longer creates the main branch. For a table that has no snapshot yet, creating main committed an empty snapshot, and every writer subtask that reached the new table before the first data commit added another one.
Why
findOrCreateBranch calls table.manageSnapshots().createBranch(branch).commit() whenever the metadata cache does not list the branch. A new table has no main ref, so the cache never lists it before the first commit, and SnapshotManager.createBranch(String) on a table without a current snapshot does transaction.newFastAppend().toBranch(name).commit() (core, SnapshotManager.java, "Create an empty snapshot for the branch"). Concurrent subtasks each pass the "ref does not exist" check and each commit their own empty snapshot. A job with parallelism 5 left up to five empty append snapshots (total-records=0, no flink.job-id) ahead of the first data snapshot.
Change
Return early from findOrCreateBranch for SnapshotRef.MAIN_BRANCH. The first commit to a table creates main, and DynamicCommitter already handles a branch with no snapshot (latestSnapshot != null ? ancestorsOf(...) : List.of()). Other branches are created as before.
The change and its test are identical in the three Flink version directories: v1.20, v2.2, v2.3.
Why only main
For another branch, createBranch(name) on a table that has a snapshot only adds a ref at the table's head and commits nothing, so there is no empty snapshot to avoid, and skipping it would make the branch start empty instead of from the head. On a table without a snapshot it does commit an empty snapshot on that branch, but that snapshot currently also gives the branch its own history: without it, the first commit to the branch is validated by DynamicCommitter's MaxCommittedCheckpointIdValidator against the ancestry that SnapshotUtil.latestSnapshot(metadata, branch) returns for a branch that does not exist, which is the head of main. If main has already committed the same job and operator for that checkpoint, the commit to the new branch is treated as a duplicate and skipped. I reproduced this by also skipping creation for other branches: TestDynamicIcebergSink#testMultipleBranches then lost the commit to branch1 in about one run in four. For main a missing ref has no ancestry to fall back to, so the early return is safe. Handling the other branches would need the committer to validate against the branch's own ancestry first, which is a separate change.
Testing

New TestTableUpdater#testMainBranchIsNotCreatedAsAnEmptySnapshot: updating a table that does not exist, twice, leaves it with no snapshots and no refs. It fails on current main (one empty append snapshot) and passes with the change.
TestTableUpdater passes in all three versions (15 tests each); spotlessApply is clean.
title: Flink: Dynamic Sink: Do not create the main branch as an empty snapshot

Equality deletes keyed on a fixed(L) column match almost nothing when the delete file is read with container reuse.
GenericParquetReaders.FixedReader.read(byte[] reuse) fills and returns the caller's reuse buffer, so every row hands back the same byte[], overwritten in place. body:
Closes #18619.
Problem
An equality delete keyed on a uuid column (most visibly a composite key like (uuid, int)) is never attached to any FileScanTask.deletes(), so none of its rows are deleted. The loaded delete set is correct; the delete file simply never reaches the reader because scan planning decides it cannot apply.
Root cause is the UUID comparator. Comparators maps UUIDType to Comparator.naturalOrder(), i.e. java.util.UUID.compareTo, which compares the two halves as signed longs:
.put(Types.UUIDType.get(), Comparator.naturalOrder())
But UUIDs are serialized and bounded as 16-byte big-endian values (spec Appendix B/D), and Parquet computes a data file's min/max bounds over those bytes in unsigned order. So a data file's stored [lower, upper] uuid bounds form an unsigned interval.
When that interval straddles the signed boundary — the most significant long of either bound is negative as a signed long, i.e. the leading byte is >= 0x80, which is roughly half of all random UUIDs — the signed comparator sees lower > upper and treats the interval as inverted. In DeleteFileIndex.canContainEqDeletesForFile → rangesOverlap, the range check then concludes the delete cannot overlap the data file and the delete is dropped. With a composite (uuid, int) key the false per-field result ANDs into the whole check, so the delete is excluded reliably. Single-column (int) / (string) controls work because their comparators match their byte serialization.
Fix
Order UUIDType with an unsigned 128-bit comparator — Long.compareUnsigned on the most significant bits, then the least — which matches the big-endian unsigned order the bounds are computed and serialized in. This fixes the mismatch for every uuid bounds comparison (delete planning, manifest pruning, ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter, residual evaluation), not just this one call site.
It is a change to UUID sort order, but toward the spec-mandated big-endian unsigned order; the only behavior that relied on the previous signed order was relying on the bug.
Tests

TestComparators.testUuid: adds pairs that cross the signed/unsigned boundary (e.g. 7fff.. < 8000.., 00.. < ff.., and an MSB tie that falls through to the least significant bits). These fail under the old signed comparator and pass with the fix. The pre-existing pair is kept and still holds (both of its UUIDs sort the same way signed or unsigned, which is why the bug went unnoticed).
DeleteFileIndexTestBase.testEqualityDeleteWithUuidKeyAttachesToDataFile: an end-to-end scan-planning test. A data file whose uuid bounds [00..01, ff..fe] straddle the boundary, and a (uuid, int) equality delete whose uuid key c0.. lies inside the range only under unsigned ordering, must be attached (forDataFile(...).hasSize(1)). Fails under the old comparator (the delete is dropped), passes with the fix. Runs under every parameterized format version in the base, so it covers the local and REST scan-planning subclasses.

Are there any user-facing changes?
No API or user-facing changes.

On v3+ tables, RowDelta validates that no concurrent commit added a DV for any data file it adds a DV for. When no starting snapshot is set, this walks the whole branch history and fails with Cannot determine history between starting snapshot null and the last known ancestor once the oldest snapshot is expired. DVs for data files added in the same commit can't conflict with concurrent commits, so the history walk is now skipped when every added DV references a data file added in that commit.
Note that the old check also incidentally rejected replays of commits with DVs, as long as history back to the original commit was available. With this change such a replay succeeds and leaves two DVs for the same data file, which makes reads fail. Iceberg doesn't reject duplicate data files in general, so preventing replays remains the committer's responsibility.
On v3 tables, this also changes the retry of an operation whose earlier attempt was applied but reported as failed: if all of its DVs reference data files added by the same operation, the retry no longer fails this check and, unless another validation rejects it, takes the existing no-op path for an already-committed snapshot. The general fix for this retry case, covering failures from any validation, is being developed in #18407.

body:
Port and enhancement of #18459 across Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1, and 4.2.
When Puffin statistics files are used for CBO, SparkScan.estimateStatistics maps blob metadata field IDs to column names using column names from the table.
Resolving field IDs against the table schema or table snapshot schema causes inaccuracies and failures:

Schema Evolution / Renames: Schema-only column renames retain the same snapshot, but Spark resolves stats by column name. If stats were mapped to historical names rather than active scan names, stats would be mismatched or fail lookup.
Time Travel & Historical Snapshots: Using the active scan schema (expectedSchema() in 3.5/4.0; schema() in 4.1/4.2) ensures field IDs map directly to the projected column names exposed by the scan.
Dropped / Missing Columns: If columns present when the Puffin file was written are absent or dropped from the active scan schema, scanSchema.findColumnName(fieldId) returns null.
Empty Blob Fields: Blobs with empty field lists (such as table-level blobs) caused index errors.

This change:

Filters out empty blob fields before grouping (filter(metadata -> !metadata.fields().isEmpty())).
Resolves column names against the active scan schema (expectedSchema() in Spark 3.5 and 4.0; schema() in Spark 4.1 and 4.2).
Safely skips fields if scanSchema.findColumnName(fieldId) returns null.
Adds comprehensive unit tests in TestSparkScan across Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1, and 4.2 verifying that stats are correctly mapped after column renames and that dropped columns are gracefully skipped without errors.
title: Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2: Use scan schema for CBO column statistics

body:
Backport of #18459 to Spark 4.2.
When Puffin statistics files are used for CBO, SparkScan.estimateStatistics maps blob metadata field IDs to column names using table.schema().findColumnName(fieldId).
If columns were dropped in a later snapshot while the statistics file belongs to the older snapshot, table.schema().findColumnName returns null, causing an NPE or unexpected error.
Furthermore, blob metadata with empty fields (e.g. table-level blobs) caused index errors.
This change:

Filters out empty blob fields before grouping (filter(metadata -> !metadata.fields().isEmpty())).
Retrieves the snapshot schema (SnapshotUtil.schemaFor(table, snapshot.snapshotId())) to resolve field IDs accurately against the snapshot's state when stats were generated.
Adds a unit test verifying statistics mapping after column drop.
title: Spark 4.2: Use snapshot schema for CBO column statistics

When connector options are used without a caller-owned catalog, FlinkDynamicTableFactory creates a temporary FlinkCatalog but leaves its underlying catalog open after extracting a loader, including when database or table operations fail. This can leak catalog-owned FileIO and client resources. Make FlinkCatalog implement AutoCloseable using its existing close() method and scope both temporary-catalog paths with try-with-resources. Caller-owned catalogs remain open, loaders can create independent catalog instances, and cleanup failures are suppressed behind an existing operation failure. Applies to Flink 1.20, 2.2, and 2.3.
Test plan and validation (JDK 17):

Verify source/sink creation, existing tables, and dynamic sinks release temporary catalogs while returned loaders remain usable; verify caller-owned catalogs stay open.

body:
Summary
To avoid rebuilding the index for every trigger, the planner has logic to reuse the
PK index between triggers. This PR fixes cases where the index can be incomplete, even
though the planner would consider the index fresh.
These cases are:

An index update fails on a trigger with nothing to convert. There are no retries,
because only triggers that convert a staging snapshot are planned again.
A job restores from a checkpoint taken before a conversion commit. The index
does not have the rows of that commit, and commits by other writers before it
are missed.
A rebuild fails half way in the planner and is still marked as done.
A conversion fails while the target branch has no snapshot yet. The retry
resolves its equality deletes against the rows the failed attempt indexed.

Constraints
All of these issues stem from two constraints of ConvertEqualityDeletes:
A. Conversion commits are made independently of the Flink checkpointing interval
B. Any failures in the conversion process must not fail the Flink job
Changes in this PR
Now the planner checks the target branch before it uses the index. The index is
used only if the head of the target branch is the snapshot the index was built
at, or the conversion commit of the last planned staging snapshot directly on
top of it. In every other case the planner rebuilds the index.
A rebuild forgets the indexed snapshot first and records the new one only after
it has emitted all read commands. A rebuild that fails half way is therefore
repeated, also after a restore. While the target branch has no snapshot, every
trigger starts a new index generation, a counter that goes up with each
rebuild. The workers drop the rows indexed so far when the generation changes.
If an index update fails in a reader or worker, the committer keeps the failed
generation in its checkpointed state and does not commit a conversion on it.
The next trigger plans the same staging snapshot again on a rebuilt index. On a
trigger with nothing to convert, this wastes one conversion unless the index is
rebuilt in between. We accept that, because we do not want to fail the job.

Developed with AI assistance. Every change was fully reviewed.
title: Flink: ConvertEqualityDeletes: Fix index consistency after a failure or restore

When a table's schema changes mid-checkpoint, DynamicWriter opens a second TaskWriter for it. When a catalog vends more than one GCS credential, OAuth2RefreshCredentialsHandler rejects the refresh response with "only one GCS credential should exist", and long-running jobs fail when the first token expires. The REST spec allows more than one credential of the same type and says clients should choose the longest matching prefix. GCSFileIO already builds one storage client per credential prefix, but the refresh handler does not know which prefix its client serves. This passes the storage prefix to the handler, which picks the longest credential prefix that the storage prefix starts with. With a single credential, the handler behaves as before. The change adds two public overloads because PrefixedStorage and GCPAuthUtils are in different packages. Follows up on #12591.
Test plan:

More than one GCS credential: the handler picks the longest prefix that covers the storage prefix and skips a longer one that does not cover it.
More than one GCS credential and none covers the storage prefix: the refresh fails.
One GCS credential: the handler uses it even when its prefix does not cover the storage prefix, so catalogs that send one credential behave as before.
GCSFileIO with two storage credentials refreshes each prefix client with its own credential. This test fails without the change.
Also checked against a real GCS bucket, before and after the change. Polaris, Lakekeeper, Gravitino and Unity Catalog send one credential and behaved the same. Nessie with projectnessie/nessie#13128 sends two, and its refresh went from failing to working. The refreshed tokens kept their table scope.

An external commit on the target branch, typically a compaction, makes the next
trigger clear the PK index and read every data file of the target again. A
compaction typically rewrites a small part of the table, but the rebuild reads
and writes all data.
With this PR, the planner applies only the data file changes of the external
commits since the indexed snapshot. The index adds the rows of every added file
and evicts the rows of every removed file. A file that is added and removed
within the range is skipped.
The planner still rebuilds the index when the incremental path does not work, in
the following cases:

There is no index yet.
The indexed snapshot is no longer in the history of the target head (rollback,
replace-main, snapshot expiration).
A planned staging snapshot has no conversion commit. Its eq deletes consumed
index entries, which a delta cannot restore.
The history has a conversion commit for another staging snapshot, for example
after a restore from a checkpoint taken before it.
The delta reads more rows than a rebuild. The planner compares the manifest list
row counts of the external commits with those of the target head. A manifest
without row counts also rebuilds.

Developed with AI assistance. Every change was fully reviewed.
title: Flink: ConvertEqualityDeletes: Add support for incremental re-indexing

Follow-up to #18610, as suggested by @mxm in #18610 (comment).
StructLikeSerializer.serializeKey(StructLike, StructType) required values in Iceberg's internal representation, but the readers pass generic Records, which hold java.time values. That mismatch caused #18609, and the only safeguard after #18610 is a javadoc note at the call site.
This PR makes the key API type-safe:

New RecordSerializer, constructed with the key StructType. It owns the InternalRecordWrapper (created once) and exposes only serializeKey(Record key), so callers can no longer pass non-internal values.
StructLikeSerializer keeps only the partition encoding (encodePartition / decodePartition). Partition tuples from ContentFile.partition() already hold internal values, so they stay StructLike-based, and DVPosition, EqualityConvertDVWriter and their tests are unchanged. Both classes share one writeField, so the byte format is defined in one place.
EqualityConvertReader no longer wraps records itself.

The serialized key format is unchanged, which matters because SerializedEqualityValues is Flink keyed state.
Testing
New TestRecordSerializer covers every primitive type with generic Java values (boolean, int, long, float, double, date, time, timestamp, timestamptz, timestamp_ns, timestamptz_ns, string, uuid, fixed, binary, decimal), with and without nulls. Each case compares the output byte-for-byte with an independent reference encoder of the previous format, built from internal values computed without the wrapper. It also checks that equivalent records produce equal keys and that a trailing _pos column on data-file records is ignored. The key tests moved out of TestStructLikeSerializer; its partition tests are unchanged.

Follow-up to #18610, answering @pvary's question in #18610 (nested equality columns such as a.b).
Depends on #18721. This branch is stacked on it; until #18721 merges, the diff here also shows its commit. Only the last commit, "Flink: Support nested equality fields in ConvertEqualityDeletes", belongs to this PR. I will rebase once #18721 is in.
Current behavior
ConvertEqualityDeletes accepts a nested equality column such as user.id, but every cycle fails in the reader:
java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Cannot serialize type: STRUCT
  at org.apache.iceberg.types.Conversions.toByteBuffer(Conversions.java:145)
  at org.apache.iceberg.flink.maintenance.operator.StructLikeSerializer.writeField(...)
  at ...EqualityConvertReader.processDataFile(...)

TypeUtil.select keeps the parent struct around a nested key field, so the key serializer received a struct value. The error aborts the cycle; no wrong keys are produced.
Change

RecordSerializer exposes the key to the byte encoder as its primitive leaf fields in depth-first schema order (new package-private FlattenedEqualityKey). This matches how core's DeleteFilter / StructProjection apply equality deletes on nested fields. A leaf under a null parent struct is serialized as null.
A key made of top-level fields only flattens to the original key type, so the serialized format (Flink keyed state) is unchanged; the existing byte-identity tests in TestRecordSerializer pass unmodified.
The builder now fails fast if an equality column is not a primitive (e.g. user) or is nested in a list or map (e.g. tags.element), and the javadoc documents this.

Testing

TestConvertEqualityDeletes: end to end, an equality delete on user.id is converted to a DV and removes the right rows; rejection of user and tags.element.
TestEqualityConvertReader: the data-row key equals the delete key for {id, user.id}; a non-matching row produces a different key.
TestRecordSerializer: exact bytes for {id, user.id, user.birthday} (including a DATE leaf) and null leaves under a null parent struct.
TestFlattenedEqualityKey: depth-first order, null parent, top-level keys unchanged, list rejected.

body:
Summary
Parquet reads the footer by seeking to the end of the file for the footer length and magic, then seeking backward to read the footer (ParquetFileReader.readFooter). For FileIO streams backed by object stores this is two sequential GET requests per file. For S3InputStream, the backward seek also aborts the first, partially read HTTP stream, so the second request opens a new connection and pays a new TLS handshake.
This change reads the footer with a single RangeReadable.readTail call when the stream supports it, which covers S3, GCS, and ADLS:

Read the last 64 KiB of the file, or the whole file if it is smaller. 64 KiB matches the default footer read size of the Arrow C++ Parquet reader.
If the footer is larger than that, issue one more readTail of exactly footer length + 8 bytes.
Parse the footer with Parquet's own public ParquetFileReader.readFooter(InputFile, ParquetReadOptions, SeekableInputStream) over an in-memory stream of those bytes. Parquet still validates length, magic, and footer position, applies the read options' metadata filter (row-group range), and handles encrypted footers.
Open the reader with the existing ParquetFileReader(InputFile, ParquetMetadata, ParquetReadOptions, SeekableInputStream) constructor. ParquetFileReader(InputFile, ParquetReadOptions, SeekableInputStream) already does exactly this internally (this(file, readFooter(file, options, f, true), options, f)); only the source of the footer bytes changes.
Streams that are not RangeReadable keep the current path unchanged: Hadoop streams, AesGcmInputStream, and in-memory streams.

Because ReadBuilder always enables vectored IO, and ParquetRangeReadableInputStreamAdapter serves readVectored with positioned reads, the sequential stream is no longer used at all when reading through ReadConf. Each file now costs one tail request plus row-group range requests, instead of two sequential footer requests plus an aborted connection plus the row-group requests.
This complements #17284 (eager fetch of files ≤ 1 MiB) for files above the eager-fetch threshold. Below the threshold the stream is the in-memory EagerInputStream, so the tail read costs no extra request.
Motivation
We found this while profiling a Spark rewrite_data_files workload on S3 that reads many small and medium files. In sampled executor thread dumps, task threads spent a large share of wall time blocked in ReadConf.newReader → ParquetFileReader.readFooter → S3InputStream.openStream. The time split between the two footer requests, and there were TLS handshake frames from the reopened connection. The cost is per file, so it dominates when files are small and numerous.
Testing
New TestParquetFooterRead:

A small footer is read with a single tail read and no seek-and-read on the stream.
A footer larger than 64 KiB (2,000-column file) uses exactly two tail reads: 64 KiB, then footer length + 8.
An end-to-end Parquet.read of a file above the eager-fetch threshold makes no sequential reads; row groups use positioned reads.
Streams without range reads fall back to the existing path.
A non-Parquet file still fails with Parquet's is not a Parquet file error, and the stream is closed.

Existing tests:

./gradlew :iceberg-parquet:check: 784 tests, plus checkstyle, error-prone, and spotless.
:iceberg-data:test --tests '*Parquet*': 146 tests.

Notes for reviewers

The 64 KiB read size is a constant, not a read property. I'm happy to make it configurable if preferred.
The change relies on each RangeReadable.readTail returning exactly the requested bytes when the request is no larger than the file. A short read raises EOFException. Like the existing path and EagerInputFile, it trusts InputFile.getLength(), which may come from manifest metadata.
Follow-up: ParquetUtil.fileMetrics, which reads only the footer (used by TableMigrationUtil), could use ParquetIO.open too. I kept this PR focused on the read path.
